blind_target.authors: Fast, N. J., Sivanathan, N., Mayer, N. D., & Galinsky, A. D.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Building from these ﬁndings, Fast and colleagues (2012)
reported ﬁve experiments that used multiple instantiations of power – including manip-
ulations via episodic recall tasks, role assignment, and extant work related power –
where they found high power to be associated with overconﬁdent decision-making.
Based on these ﬁndings, we propose that exaggerated expressions of conﬁdence will
emerge as a function of the degree to which high-power poses facilitate a high-power
mind-set.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
High-power (M = 0.14, SD = 0.53) posers did not have higher post-manipulation levels of
overconﬁdence than low-power posers (M = −0.01, SD = 0.51), F(1,104) = 0.26, p = 0.61,
d = 0.099, r = 0.05.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The extension directly tests the published power-to-overconfidence relationship using embodied power. The introduction states the original positive finding and derives this study’s prediction from it; the new-sample comparison fails to show it. This is a conceptual retest, even though called an extension.
blind_target.title: Power and overconﬁdent decision-making.

blind_target.authors: Mehta, P. H., Welker, K. M., Zilioli, S., & Carré, J. M.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Because Carney et al.
(2010) found high-power poses to both increase testosterone and decrease cortisol, the
interaction between these eﬀects may predict risk-taking, as has been previously shown
(Mehta et al., 2015). Furthermore, although Ranehill et al. (2015) failed to replicate
Carney et al.’s (2010) eﬀects of power posing on hormonal changes, other manipulations
related to power, such as winning a competition, have been shown to jointly impact
testosterone and cortisol (e.g. see Hamilton, Carré, Mehta, Olmstead, & Whitaker, 2015).
Thus, in the present research, we measured both testosterone and cortisol at two time
points, as per Carney et al.’s (2010) original design and tested for both main and
interactive eﬀects.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
The interaction
between post-manipulation testosterone and cortisol was also unrelated to gambling
decisions, z = 0.02, p = 0.90, φ = 0.037.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The paper explicitly invokes the previously shown testosterone-by-cortisol prediction of risk-taking, then measures both hormones to test their interactive effects in its own sample. The corresponding interaction is unrelated to gambling decisions, contrary to that published prediction.
blind_target.title: Testosterone and cortisol jointly modulate risk-taking.

parent_scope_objection: Second and final review, initial1spent per key. Initial exclusions call Fast2012power-overconfidence and Mehta2015testosterone-by-cortisol/risk findings merely motivation for a novel mediation extension. Current primary rationale explicitly attributes empirical power-overconfidence association toFast and dualhormoneinteraction/risk association toMehta2015, then measures overconfidence and BOTHhormones and tests main/interactive paths on newdata. A new powerposing manipulation or embedding an earlierfinding in a novelmediationmodel does not automatically eliminate its specific empirical retest; a method citation alone is insufficient too. For EACH earlierpaper establish the actual original-specific claim and whether a measured/tested current path re-tests it, or whether current hormonechanges/powerconstruct/context represent a substantively differenthypothesis. Do not equate generic modelrationale with every empiricaltarget; do not require the authors to call the addedtest replication or recite the citation in Discussion.
